groups.high: ICCPR Article 14(3)(g) protects a person facing a criminal charge from being compelled to testify against themselves or confess guilt. The Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 32 addresses direct or indirect physical and undue psychological pressure by investigating authorities. It connects the safeguard to Article 7's prohibition of torture and ill-treatment. A confession obtained through prohibited coercion must not be used to establish guilt; an allegation of coercion requires proper examination. Voluntary admissions are not categorically forbidden, and the exact treatment of non-testimonial physical evidence or legally sufficient immunity requires its own legal analysis. The prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt; a compelled confession must not replace independent evidence and a fair defense. Article 14(2)'s presumption of innocence reinforces this allocation. US Fifth Amendment and Miranda rules are related domestic protections but are not identical to the ICCPR or the origin of the universal treaty rule. Compulsory self-incrimination is also distinct from double jeopardy, which concerns repeated prosecution or punishment after a final judgment. Access to counsel and fair interrogation safeguards help prevent unreliable admissions and abuse. The aim is not to prevent investigation but to ensure that the state proves its case lawfully without forcing the accused to supply a confession.
groups.mid: Article 14(3)(g) of the ICCPR says a person charged with a crime must not be forced to testify against themselves or confess guilt. This covers physical force and undue mental pressure. The Human Rights Committee explains it in General Comment No. 32. Article 7 also bans torture and ill-treatment. A confession gained through prohibited pressure must not be used to prove guilt. A claim of coercion needs a proper check. A person can still choose to speak freely. Rules about physical evidence, or a promise of legal immunity, need separate legal advice. The state must prove guilt. It must not replace evidence with a forced confession. Article 14(2) protects the presumption of innocence too. In the US, the Fifth Amendment and Miranda rules offer related safeguards. They are not the same as the ICCPR and did not create the treaty rule. Double jeopardy is different: it concerns a second trial or punishment after a final result. Legal advice and fair questioning help protect against forced or false admissions. This right does not stop lawful investigation. It requires the state to build its case fairly rather than force the accused to confess.
groups.low: If you face a criminal charge, you must not be forced to confess. You must not be forced to give evidence against yourself. Article 14(3)(g) of the ICCPR protects this right. Force can be physical. Undue mental pressure can count too. The Human Rights Committee explains this in General Comment No. 32. Article 7 bans torture and ill-treatment. A confession obtained through prohibited pressure must not be used to prove guilt. If someone says they were forced, that claim needs a proper check. A person may still choose to speak freely. Physical evidence and legal immunity have separate rules. Ask a lawyer about them. The state has to prove guilt. It cannot use a forced confession in place of a fair case. Article 14(2) says the accused is presumed innocent. The US Fifth Amendment and Miranda rules are related, but they are not identical to the ICCPR. Double jeopardy is another right. It deals with a second trial or punishment after a final result. A lawyer and fair rules for questioning help prevent abuse and false admissions. The police may still investigate. They must do so lawfully, not force you to confess.
groups.source_review: Article14(3)(g), GC32 coercion interpretation and related7/14(2) checked.
groups.notes: Removed false double-jeopardy connection and blanket immunity claim; distinguished US domestic rules.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 9(4) entitles anyone deprived of liberty by arrest or detention to challenge its lawfulness before a court. The court must decide without delay and order release if detention is unlawful. Habeas corpus is a familiar domestic mechanism for this protection, but the treaty guarantee is not limited to systems using that name. It applies beyond ordinary criminal imprisonment, including relevant immigration and other detention. A legal challenge must be practical: access to advice, communication, necessary information, and an independent court can be essential. A formal law or warrant is not enough if detention is arbitrary or otherwise incompatible with the Covenant. The right differs from Article 9(3)'s automatic prompt appearance before a judge following a criminal arrest; a request-based challenge under paragraph 4 must not be confused with that separate duty. Review should address the actual grounds and continuing justification, with further review where circumstances require. The court must have meaningful power to order release, not merely issue a nonbinding recommendation. Domestic deadlines and procedure vary, but cannot defeat the without-delay requirement. This safeguard checks executive power and can expose incommunicado detention, ill-treatment, or disappearance. It does not guarantee release when detention is lawful, and specialist advice is needed about the appropriate court and remedies.
groups.mid: Article 9(4) of the ICCPR gives a detained person a right to ask a court to check if the detention is lawful. The court must decide without delay. If it is unlawful, the court must order release. Habeas corpus is one name for this kind of safeguard. The right is not limited to countries that use that name. It can apply to immigration and other detention, not just jail after a criminal charge. The person needs a real way to bring the case. Advice, contact with others, relevant information, and an independent court may be needed. A law or warrant does not settle everything: detention can still be arbitrary or breach the Covenant. Article 9(3) is different. It requires a prompt appearance before a judge after a criminal arrest, without waiting for the person to ask. Article 9(4) protects a challenge to detention. Review must check the real grounds. It must check any continuing need to hold the person too. Further checks may be needed as facts change. The court must be able to order release, not just suggest it. Local procedures differ, but must not cause undue delay. This helps guard against hidden detention, abuse, and disappearance. It does not promise release if detention is lawful. Ask about the right court and available remedies.
groups.low: If you are detained, you can ask a court to check whether it is lawful. Article 9(4) of the ICCPR protects this. The court must act without delay. It must order release if the detention is unlawful. This safeguard is often called habeas corpus. A country does not have to use that name for the right to apply. It covers more than criminal jail. It can cover immigration and other detention too. You need a real way to ask. Legal advice, contact with others, and key facts about the case may help. The court must be independent. A warrant or a law alone does not prove all detention is fair. It may still be arbitrary or breach the Covenant. Article 9(3) is a separate rule. After a criminal arrest, a person must be brought promptly before a judge. They do not have to ask first. Under Article 9(4), the court checks the actual grounds and whether they still justify holding the person. A new review may be needed if facts change. The court must have power to release, not just offer advice. Local steps differ, but delay must not defeat the right. This can help expose hidden detention, abuse, or disappearance. It does not promise release when detention is lawful. Ask for advice about the right court.
groups.source_review: Article9(4) and distinction from9(3) checked; practical court remedy framed independently of writ label.
groups.notes: Corrected conflation of automatic production before judge with court challenge initiated by detainee.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 14(2) requires everyone charged with a criminal offense to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law. The prosecution bears the burden of proving the charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused benefits from doubt; this is not a demand for logically absolute certainty. A person need not prove innocence or cure gaps in the prosecution case. Evidence must be assessed through a fair process rather than rumor, publicity, or institutional assumptions of guilt. Public authorities must avoid statements prejudging guilt, and media coverage should not undermine a fair trial. Arrest or pretrial detention is not itself a conviction. Detention must have lawful, individualized justification rather than operate as punishment based on presumed guilt. Other safeguards include an impartial tribunal, access to defense, the ability to challenge evidence, and protection from compelled self-incrimination. The presumption does not prohibit investigating reasonable suspicion or imposing every lawful precaution. Nor does it alone settle every private statement or civil dispute. Officials must distinguish allegation from established guilt and avoid presenting an accused person as already convicted. The protection matters because premature judgments can damage liberty, reputation, employment, and family life even where a case ultimately fails. Its function is a fair allocation of proof, not philosophical certainty about facts before trial.
groups.mid: Article 14(2) of the ICCPR says a person charged with a crime is presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law. The prosecution must prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The accused benefits from doubt and does not have to prove innocence. This does not mean proof must reach absolute certainty. A fair court should assess evidence, not rumors, public anger, or an assumption that arrest means guilt. Officials must not speak as if guilt is already decided. News coverage should not undermine a fair trial. Being arrested or held before trial is not the same as being convicted. Detention needs lawful reasons based on the person's case. It must not be punishment in advance. An impartial court, time and help to defend the case, a chance to challenge evidence, and protection from forced confession support this right. Police can still investigate reasonable suspicion. It does not ban every lawful precaution or settle every private statement or civil claim. The key is to keep an allegation separate from proved guilt. Calling a person guilty too soon can harm their freedom, job, good name, and family even if the case later fails. The state must prove its case through a fair process.
groups.low: A charge is not proof of guilt. Article 14(2) of the ICCPR says an accused person is presumed innocent until proved guilty by law. The prosecution must prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. If there is such doubt, it helps the accused. The person does not have to prove innocence. Beyond reasonable doubt is not the same as absolute certainty. A court must use evidence, not rumors or public anger. Officials must not say guilt is already settled. News reports should not damage a fair trial. An arrest is not a conviction. Being held before trial is not proof either. Detention needs lawful reasons for that person's case. It must not punish someone in advance. A fair judge, help with the defense, a chance to question evidence, and no forced confession all support the right. Police can still investigate reasonable suspicion. The rule does not ban every lawful precaution. It also does not decide every private remark or civil case. Keep claims and proved facts separate. Calling a person guilty too soon can damage their job, name, family, and freedom even if the case fails. The state must prove guilt fairly.
groups.source_review: Article14(2) and GC32 burden/doubt/public-authority safeguards checked.
groups.notes: Corrected absolute-certainty claim and overly broad ban on any pretrial treatment as suspect.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 14(7) protects against renewed trial or punishment for an offense after a final conviction or acquittal in accordance with the country's law and penal procedure. The principle is often called double jeopardy or ne bis in idem. Finality matters: an ordinary appeal or a retrial ordered after reversal is not automatically a second prohibited prosecution. Human Rights Committee General Comment No. 32 distinguishes exceptional reopening, such as where previously unavailable evidence is discovered, from an unrestricted power to relitigate a final case. Merely changing the charge's label must not become a way to evade the protection, but whether matters constitute the same offense requires legal assessment. The Covenant guarantee is primarily concerned with repeated proceedings within the same state; it does not itself establish a universal bar to prosecution in another country. Domestic or regional law may provide broader protection. Distinct offenses, invalid proceedings, and exceptional reopening require careful analysis rather than assuming every statutory exception is valid. The rule protects legal certainty, limits harassment through repeated prosecution, and preserves the meaning of a final acquittal or conviction. It is not permission to avoid lawful appeal, nor a guarantee that all proceedings worldwide about related conduct are barred. Check the judgment's finality, jurisdiction, offense, and applicable review rules.
groups.mid: Article 14(7) of the ICCPR protects against another trial or punishment for an offense after a final conviction or acquittal under the country's law. This is called double jeopardy, or ne bis in idem. A final judgment matters. A normal appeal or a retrial ordered after a judgment is overturned is not automatically a breach. The Human Rights Committee explains in General Comment No. 32 that exceptional reopening, such as discovery of evidence not available before, differs from simply trying a final case again. A state must not evade the right just by changing the label on the same charge. But deciding what counts as the same offense needs legal care. This treaty rule mainly concerns repeated cases within one state. It does not itself stop every other country from bringing a case about the same conduct. Local or regional law may protect more. A separate offense, an invalid first case, or a proposed reopening must be checked under the relevant law. A national law calling something an exception does not automatically make it valid under the Covenant. The right limits harassment and gives final decisions meaning. It does not abolish lawful appeals or block every related case worldwide. Check finality, the offense, the country, and review rules.
groups.low: Double jeopardy is a rule against another trial or punishment. It concerns the same offense after a final result. Article 14(7) of the ICCPR gives the right. The first case must have a final result under the country's law. It must be a conviction or acquittal. A conviction finds the person guilty. An acquittal finds them not guilty. Final means the case has reached the stage the law treats as settled. An ordinary appeal can still be part of the case. That is not the same as starting again after a final result. A normal appeal is not automatically a second forbidden trial. A court may also order a new trial when a judgment is overturned. General Comment No. 32 explains the limits. A final case can sometimes be reopened for exceptional reasons. One example is evidence not available before. This is not a free right to keep trying again. Changing a charge's name must not be a trick to avoid the rule. What is the same offense needs legal advice. The treaty rule mainly works within one state. It does not itself stop every other country from bringing a case. Local or regional law may give more protection. A different offense, an invalid first trial, or new evidence needs careful checks. A law calling something an exception does not settle whether it meets the Covenant. The rule stops the state wearing people down with repeated cases. It makes a final decision count. It does not end lawful appeals. Check the final result, offense, country, and review rules.
groups.source_review: Article14(7), GC32 exceptional reopening and interstate limitation checked.
groups.notes: Added territorial scope and qualified reopening instead of unrestricted statutory exception.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 14(3)(b) guarantees adequate time and facilities to prepare a criminal defense and communicate with counsel of one's choosing. Article 14(3)(d) separately protects presence at trial, defense in person or through chosen legal assistance, information about the right where counsel is absent, and assigned counsel where the interests of justice require it. Such assigned assistance must be free when the person lacks sufficient means. This does not give every defendant unlimited public funding or an unconditional right to any particular publicly funded lawyer. Time and facilities depend on the case's needs, including access to relevant documents, evidence, confidential consultation, and an opportunity to prepare effective responses. Communication with counsel must be practically possible and protected against improper interference. Appointing a lawyer in name only does not ensure an effective defense; authorities must respond to manifest failures requiring intervention, while not every strategic error is attributable to the state. Preparation and access concerns should be raised promptly with counsel and the court, including requests for time where needed. The right supports equality of arms and the presumption of innocence. It is not limited to a guaranteed favorable verdict, nor should it be described as automatically invalidating every outcome without analysis of the violation and remedy.
groups.mid: Article 14(3)(b) of the ICCPR gives a person enough time and facilities to prepare a criminal defense and speak with a lawyer they choose. Article 14(3)(d) covers being present at trial, defending yourself or using chosen legal help, and being told about that right. A lawyer must be assigned if the interests of justice require it. This help must be free if the person lacks enough money. It does not mean unlimited funding or a right to any chosen state-paid lawyer. The needs depend on the case. The person may need papers, evidence, and private talks with counsel. They also need time to answer the state's case. Officials must not improperly block contact with the lawyer. A name on a form is not enough if no real defense is provided. Authorities must respond to clear failures that call for action. But not every mistake in a lawyer's strategy is the state's fault. Raise missing evidence, lack of private contact, or too little time with counsel and the court promptly. Extra time may be needed. These rights help make the trial fair and support the presumption of innocence. They do not promise a win, or make every possible remedy automatic.
groups.low: If you face a criminal charge, you need time and help to defend yourself. Article 14(3)(b) of the ICCPR protects time to prepare and contact with a lawyer you choose. Article 14(3)(d) protects being at trial and using a lawyer or defending yourself. You must be told about the right if you have no lawyer. The state must assign one when the interests of justice require it. It must be free if you cannot afford it. This is not a right to unlimited funds or any lawyer you name at state cost. What you need depends on the case. You may need key papers, evidence, private talks, and time to answer the charge. Officials must not wrongly block lawyer contact. Giving you a lawyer's name on paper is not enough if there is no real help. Clear failures may require action by the authorities. But not every poor choice by a lawyer is the state's fault. Tell your lawyer and the court about missing papers, lack of privacy, or too little time. Ask for more time where needed. These rights help make the trial fair. They do not promise that you will win or that every remedy is automatic.
groups.source_review: Article14(3)(b)/(d) free-assistance conditions and preparation safeguards checked.
groups.notes: Added means/interests-of-justice conditions and qualified lawyer choice/public funding.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 10(1) requires all persons deprived of liberty to be treated humanely and with respect for inherent dignity. The duty applies regardless of conviction, nationality, wealth, or alleged offense, including detention outside ordinary prisons. Loss of liberty does not extinguish other rights except restrictions inherent in lawful confinement. Authorities must provide conditions compatible with dignity, including adequate food, water, sanitation, accommodation, and healthcare, and protect against abuse by staff or other detainees. Resource shortages do not excuse inhumane treatment. Article 7 separately prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment, and is nonderogable. Article 10 complements it with positive custodial duties rather than merely repeating a ban on severe violence. Article 10(2) normally separates accused persons from convicted prisoners, subject to exceptional circumstances, and provides distinct protection for juveniles. Article 10(3) makes reformation and social rehabilitation an essential aim of the penitentiary system and requires age-appropriate separation and treatment for juvenile offenders. Access to legal remedies and oversight helps expose unlawful conditions, although arrest legality and fair-trial guarantees also arise under Articles 9 and 14. Punishment or security needs do not authorize humiliation, neglect, or the arbitrary withdrawal of essential care.
groups.mid: Article 10(1) of the ICCPR says people in custody must be treated humanely and with dignity. This is care and respect for their worth as human beings. It applies whether they are accused or convicted, rich or poor, citizens or foreigners. It covers more than ordinary prisons. Lawful custody limits freedom, not all other rights. Staff must provide adequate food, water, toilets, space, and health care. They must stop abuse by staff and other people held there. Lack of money does not excuse inhumane conditions. Article 7 separately bans torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. Even an emergency cannot cancel that ban. Article 10 requires care too. It is not enough just to avoid severe violence. Food must be fit to eat and water safe to drink. Article 10(2) normally keeps those accused apart from those already found guilty. Only exceptional cases depart from this normal rule. Young people have separate safeguards. Article 10(3) says reform and social rehabilitation must be essential aims of prison. This means help to return to life in society. Young offenders need to be kept apart. They also need care suited to their age. Ways to seek redress and checks free from improper influence can expose abuse. Articles 9 and 14 protect lawful detention and fair trials too. Security or punishment is no excuse for shaming, neglect, or denial of needed care.
groups.low: People held by the state still have rights. Article 10(1) of the ICCPR says they must be treated humanely and with dignity. This means care and respect for their worth as people. It covers rich and poor. It covers citizens and foreigners. It covers those accused and those found guilty. It covers more than prisons. Being held lawfully limits freedom. It does not erase all rights. Staff must give enough food, water, toilets, space, and health care. Food must be fit to eat. Water must be safe to drink. Toilets must be fit to use. Staff must stop abuse by staff or others held there. Lack of money does not excuse poor care. Article 7 bans torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. Even an emergency does not cancel that ban. Article 10 requires care as well. Just not using severe violence is not enough. Under Article 10(2), those accused should normally be kept apart from those found guilty. An accused person has not yet been proved guilty. Narrow exceptions exist, but this is the normal rule. Young people have separate safeguards. Article 10(3) makes reform and social rehabilitation key aims of prison. This means helping people return to life in society, not just holding them. Young offenders need to be kept apart. They need care that fits their age. A child is not just an adult. A way to seek legal redress helps expose abuse. So do checks by an independent body. Articles 9 and 14 also protect rights. They concern lawful detention and fair trials. Security or punishment does not excuse shaming or neglect. It does not excuse denial of needed care.
groups.source_review: Article10 humane treatment, separation and rehabilitation text checked; Article7 distinguished.
groups.notes: Restored Article10 attribution and its often-omitted positive and juvenile duties.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 9(3) requires anyone arrested or detained on a criminal charge to be brought promptly before a judge or other legally authorized judicial officer. The Human Rights Committee regards 48 hours as ordinarily sufficient; longer delay must be genuinely exceptional and justified. A prosecutor does not satisfy the required judicial independence merely by supervising police. Children require a particularly strict standard of promptness. The detainee is entitled to trial within a reasonable time or release; Article 14(3)(c) separately requires trial without undue delay. Pretrial detention must not be the general rule. It needs an individualized, necessary, and proportionate basis, such as demonstrated risks of flight or interference with evidence, with alternatives considered and continuing justification reviewed. Case complexity and conduct can affect reasonable time, but chronic resource shortages are not a blanket excuse. Release may be unconditional or subject to proportionate guarantees of appearance, including reporting, travel-document restrictions, or appropriate bail. Conditions must not make release illusory merely because a person is poor. Release pending trial does not end the prosecution, and bail conditions are not mandatory in every case. Article 9(4)'s right to challenge detention is distinct from the automatic prompt judicial appearance. A routine 72-hour allowance should not be substituted for the Committee's stricter guidance.
groups.mid: After a criminal arrest, a person must see a judge promptly. Article 9(3) of the ICCPR says so. Another officer may act if the law gives them the right judicial powers. The Human Rights Committee says 48 hours is usually enough. A longer wait needs an exceptional reason and must be justified. A prosecutor is not the same as a judge. The judge must be independent of the case. For children, the time standard is stricter. The person has a right to trial within a reasonable time or release. Article 14(3)(c) also bans undue trial delay. Jail before trial must not be the norm. A court needs grounds specific to the person. They may be a real risk of flight or harm to evidence. The court must consider options that limit freedom less. It must keep checking if there is still a need to hold the person. A case with hard issues may take time. A lack of court resources is not a free excuse for delay. Release can have no conditions. Or there may be reasonable steps to ensure the person comes back. These can include reporting, a passport handover, or suitable bail. Poverty must not make release impossible. Release does not end the case. Article 9(4) lets a person challenge detention separately. That is not the same as the prompt judge appearance. Do not assume a routine 72-hour wait is always lawful.
groups.low: A person arrested on a criminal charge must see a judge promptly. Article 9(3) of the ICCPR says so. An officer with the right judicial powers may also act. The Human Rights Committee says 48 hours is usually enough. A longer wait needs an exceptional reason that can be justified. A prosecutor is not the same as an independent judge who can review the case. Children need even quicker review. The person has a right to trial in a reasonable time. Or they must be released. Article 14(3)(c) also says there must be no undue delay. Holding people before trial should not be the normal rule. A court needs reasons for that person. These may include a real risk of flight or harm to evidence. It must look at options that limit freedom less. It must keep reviewing the need. A case with hard issues may take time. Too few court resources do not excuse any delay. Release may have no conditions. Or it may require steps to secure attendance. These can be reporting, a passport handover, or suitable bail. Being poor must not make release impossible. Release does not end the charge. Article 9(4) gives a separate right to challenge being held. Do not confuse it with the prompt judge review. A routine 72-hour wait is not always lawful.
groups.source_review: Article9(3), GC35 48-hour interpretation, judicial independence and release alternatives checked.
groups.notes: Corrected routine48–72-hour claim, mandatory conditions on release and resource-based delay excuse.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 15 protects legality in criminal law: an act or omission cannot be punished as criminal if it was not an offense under national or international law when it occurred. Nor may a heavier penalty be imposed than the one applicable then. If a later law provides a lighter penalty, the offender must benefit from it. This favorable-retroactivity rule is essential and should not be omitted from a summary focused only on new offenses. Article 15(2) preserves trial and punishment for conduct criminal, when committed, according to general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It does not allow inventing a crime after the event. The guarantee is nonderogable under Article 4, including during public emergencies. Predictable, accessible criminal rules protect against arbitrary state power; interpretation should not unexpectedly turn previously innocent conduct into a crime. Not every procedural change or civil rule is governed identically, so a blanket ban on all retrospective legislation would be inaccurate. Amnesty is a distinct issue, not an exception authorizing retroactive criminalization. Assess the conduct date, the then-applicable national or international offense, the penalty, and any later lighter law. The principle is often summarized as no crime and no punishment without law, or nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege.
groups.mid: Article 15 of the ICCPR says no one should be punished for an act that was not a crime when it happened. The test uses national and international law at that time. The state cannot give a heavier penalty than the one that applied then. If a later law gives a lighter penalty, the person must benefit. This is not just a ban on new crimes after the event. Article 15(2) concerns acts that were already crimes under general principles recognized by the community of nations. It allows trial for them. It does not allow a crime to be invented later. Under Article 4, an emergency cannot suspend Article 15. People need clear rules about crime so they can know what the law forbids. A later reading should not suddenly turn an innocent past act into a crime. Court procedure and civil law can follow different rules. So not every law with a past effect is banned. Amnesty is a separate matter, not permission to create a past crime. Check the act's date, the law then, the penalty, and any later lighter law. The Latin phrase nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege means no crime or punishment without law.
groups.low: You must not be punished for something that was not a crime when you did it. Article 15 of the ICCPR protects this. The test includes national and international law at that time. The state cannot give a heavier penalty than the one that applied then. If the law later provides a lighter penalty, you must get that benefit. This is an important part of the right. Article 15(2) covers acts that were already crimes under general principles recognized by the community of nations. It does not let a state invent a crime later. Under Article 4, even an emergency cannot suspend Article 15. People need clear rules so they know what is a crime. A later reading should not suddenly make an innocent past act criminal. Court procedure and civil laws can have different rules. So not every law with a past effect is banned in the same way. An amnesty is a separate issue. It does not allow a new crime to be applied to the past. Check the date of the act, the law then, the penalty then, and any later lighter penalty. The Latin phrase nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege means no crime or punishment without law.
groups.source_review: Article15 full text including lighter penalty and15(2), plus nonderogability under4, checked.
groups.notes: Added omitted lighter-penalty guarantee and international-law clause; removed amnesty-as-retroactivity-exception.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 14(1) guarantees equality before courts and a fair public hearing by a competent, independent, impartial tribunal established by law when determining criminal charges or rights and obligations in a suit at law. This is not an automatic identical hearing requirement for every administrative decision. Independence concerns freedom from improper external influence; impartiality concerns bias or a personal stake. Fairness requires a genuine opportunity to present and challenge the case, with appropriate equality of arms. Public hearings allow scrutiny by press and public. The treaty permits exclusion for morals, public order, national security in a democratic society, protection of private life, or special circumstances where strictly necessary to protect justice. These are defined exceptions, not a general secrecy license. Judgments must generally be public, with limited exceptions for juvenile interests, matrimonial disputes, and child guardianship. Written appeals or some preliminary proceedings do not always require an oral public hearing. The whole article is not expressly nonderogable under Article 4; emergency measures remain tightly constrained and cannot circumvent other nonderogable protections or essential fair-trial principles. Publicity is therefore important but not unlimited. Assess the type of proceeding, legal authority, need for any restriction, independence, and practical fairness rather than claiming openness alone guarantees justice.
groups.mid: Article 14(1) of the ICCPR protects equal access to courts and fair public hearings. The tribunal must be established by law. It must be competent, independent, and impartial. A tribunal is a body that decides a case under law. It needs lawful powers and the skills for the task. It must not be biased or act under improper outside pressure. The rule covers criminal charges and rights or duties in a suit at law. Not every administrative decision needs the same hearing. Each side needs a fair chance to explain and challenge the case. The public and press can normally attend. The treaty sets limited grounds for closure. These include morals, public order, and national security in a democratic society. Private life is another ground. Special cases can also allow closure to the extent justice strictly needs it. They are not a license to hide any trial. The public rule is the starting point, and a reason for closing the hearing must fit the legal grounds. Judgments are normally public too. Exceptions concern young people's interests. Marriage disputes and child guardianship can also qualify. Some written appeals or early procedural steps need no oral public hearing. Oral means spoken, rather than a court deciding only from the written papers. Article 14 as a whole is not listed as nonderogable under Article 4. Strict rules for emergencies still apply. Essential fair-trial principles and other rights that cannot be suspended must not be bypassed. Check the case type, the court's powers, the reason for closure, and real fairness. An open door alone is not enough.
groups.low: Courts must be fair. Article 14(1) of the ICCPR says people are equal before courts. It also gives a right to fair public hearings. The tribunal must be established by law. It must be competent, independent, and impartial. A tribunal is a body that decides a case under law. It needs lawful powers and the skills for the task. It must not be biased. It must not follow improper outside pressure. The rule covers criminal charges and rights or duties in a suit at law. It is not the same hearing rule for all administrative decisions. Both sides need a fair chance to explain and challenge the case. The press and public can normally attend. There are limited grounds to close a hearing. They include morals, public order, and national security in a democratic society. Private life is another ground. Special cases can allow closure only to the extent justice strictly needs it. This does not let officials hide any case. Start from the open-hearing rule, then ask if a legal reason for closure really fits. Judgments are normally public. Exceptions concern young people's interests. Marriage disputes and child guardianship can also qualify. Some written appeals or early steps need no oral public hearing. Oral means spoken. In some cases, judges can use written papers rather than hear everyone speak in an open room. Article 14 is not wholly listed as nonderogable under Article 4. Emergency limits still face strict rules. They cannot bypass essential fair-trial principles or other rights that cannot be suspended. Check the case, powers, reason for closure, and fairness. An open door alone is not enough.
groups.source_review: Article14(1) scope, closure/judgment exceptions, GC32 and Article4 distinction checked.
groups.notes: Corrected all-administrative-hearings claim and whole-Article14 absolute nonderogability.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 14(3)(f) guarantees free assistance of an interpreter to an accused person who cannot understand or speak the language used in court. Human Rights Committee General Comment No. 32 applies this safeguard to oral criminal proceedings, including relevant stages beyond the trial hearing. It applies to nationals and foreigners alike. A different mother tongue does not create an automatic entitlement where the accused understands the court language well enough to defend effectively. Conversely, nationality does not establish sufficient comprehension. Interpretation must be competent enough to permit meaningful understanding and participation, including communication needed for defense; poor-quality or missing assistance can undermine fairness. The accused should not be charged for required interpretation merely because they can afford it or are later convicted. This specific clause does not automatically give every civil litigant, witness, victim, or lawyer a free interpreter in every setting. Other equality, fair-hearing, or domestic-law duties may provide assistance in those situations. Nor does it promise translation of every written document regardless of necessity. Assess language needs early and raise deficiencies promptly with counsel and the court. Remedies for a violation depend on the circumstances and governing law; absence of interpretation does not mechanically render every judgment void without legal analysis. The purpose is an effective defense, not a discretionary courtesy.
groups.mid: Article 14(3)(f) of the ICCPR gives a free interpreter to an accused person who cannot understand or speak the court's language. General Comment No. 32 explains the right. It concerns oral criminal proceedings and relevant stages beyond the trial. Citizens and foreigners can both need help. A different first language does not always qualify if the person can use the court language well enough to defend the case. Being a citizen does not prove that they can. The interpreter must have suitable skills. The person must be able to understand and take part in a real way. Poor or missing help can make the trial unfair. Required help is free. The accused must not be billed just because they can pay or are later convicted. This clause does not give every civil party, witness, victim, or lawyer a free interpreter in every setting. Other laws and fairness duties may help them. It does not require every written paper to be translated regardless of need. Check needs early and tell counsel and the court about problems. A breach may need a remedy. It does not automatically make every judgment void. The aim is a real defense, not a favor.
groups.low: If you face a criminal charge, you need to understand the court's language. If you cannot understand or speak it, you have a right to a free interpreter. Article 14(3)(f) of the ICCPR protects this. An interpreter puts spoken words into another language. You can follow what is said and make your own words understood. General Comment No. 32 explains it. It covers spoken steps in a criminal case, including relevant steps beyond the trial. Oral means spoken. You need to hear and be heard in the case. Just sitting in a room without knowing what happens is not enough. It can apply to citizens or foreigners. A different first language is not enough on its own. You may use the court language well enough to defend yourself. Being a citizen does not prove you can. The interpreter needs the right skills so you can understand and take part. They must help you follow the case and make your words clear too. Poor or missing help can make the trial unfair. Help required by this right is free. You must not be billed because you have money or are later convicted. This clause does not cover every person in a civil case. Nor does it give every witness, victim, or lawyer a free interpreter in all settings. Their needs may be covered by other laws, which must be checked. It does not require all written papers in another language regardless of need. Ask early if you need help. Tell your lawyer and the court if it does not work. If the right is breached, a remedy may be needed. Not every judgment becomes void at once. The goal is a defense you can take part in.
